journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Centering diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging through Universal Design for Learning and trauma-informed pedagogy
abstract: This case study documents a student-faculty partnership within a fully online higher education Master of Education (MEd) program in the United States. A faculty advisor and three graduate students co-developed a diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging (DEIB)-centered course audit rubric grounded in Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and trauma-informed pedagogy. The team collaboratively benchmarked inclusive practices, reviewed institutional and scholarly resources, and iteratively refined the rubric through dialogue and reflection. Structured around three areas: (a) syllabus and policies, (b) course materials, and (c) assignments and assessments, the rubric offers a practical, student-informed framework for embedding equity principles into course design. Although the rubric has not yet been implemented, this initiative illustrates how student-faculty collaboration can operationalize DEIB values in pedagogical practice. The case highlights the importance of shared responsibility, reflexivity, and transparency in building inclusive learning environments and provides a replicable model for programs seeking to embed DEIB through student-faculty partnerships.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Institutional calibration, adaptation, and sustainability of pedagogical partnerships
abstract: Teams at four structurally distinct institutions of higher education calibrated and adapted the faculty-student pedagogical partnership program known as Students as Learners and Teachers (SaLT) to match the different contexts and challenges of their institutions. This cross-context case study compares these models of pedagogical partnership to reveal strategies for building trust, community, and sustainability that we hope will resonate with and inspire others who wish to develop similar programs. In particular, we highlight several strategies to rebalance power between faculty and students, as well as strategies to reduce skepticism and promote ownership of the program on the part of faculty. While all four programs face ongoing funding challenges, we also describe how the four models are sustained by reducing administrative burden, streamlining reporting by participants, and attempting to integrate the programs into pre-existing institutional structures.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Building together
abstract: Students as Partners (SaP) work and its effectiveness are well documented in the higher education literature. While there are examples of SaP in health professions education (HPE), they are limited compared to the college and university landscape. Based on student feedback, we engaged students, faculty, and staff in a co-creation process to develop a flourishing, strengths-based professional development program. This case study sought to establish a best-practices approach to SaP work in HPE by describing its unfolding at our institution and sharing results from our examination of students, faculty, and staff perspectives on SaP work at an academic medical center.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Partnership, co-creation, transformation
abstract: This case study discusses how the experience of co-creating a project in English language teacher education opened opportunities for transformative learning in a student-staff partnership between a teacher-researcher (TR) and two student assistants (SAs) at an Austrian university. The project was not a designated students as partners (SaP) initiative in which students are seen as equal contributors; however, it was implicitly designated as a learning opportunity for students by the university, albeit without any clear guidelines for implementation. This lack of direction allowed a model of student-staff co-creation to evolve organically. Data for this case study were collected in a retrospective reflection session. Through data coding and analysis, contextual factors that facilitated transformative learning for both the SAs and the TR were identified. These factors can now be taken into consideration by the TR in future project work with SAs and may also be of interest to staff working in similar contexts.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: A student-led neurodivergent peer group as praxis of access, belonging, and partnership
abstract: This case study examines the praxis of a student-led neurodivergent group founded in 2023 to address structural and interpersonal barriers to belonging, access, and community. Centered on lived experience and neuro-affirming values, the group provides weekly meetups, resources, and advocacy partnerships, with students as partners in design, facilitation, and advocacy. It demonstrates that student retention and flourishing depend not only on academic accommodations or therapeutic interventions but also on affirming peer spaces that foster connection, safety, and joy. We argue that such identity-based initiatives must be recognized as essential infrastructure for access, students-as-partners practice, and transformation in higher education.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Partnering on AI policies for upper-level humanities courses
abstract: This case study describes a process by which students authored their own generative AI (GenAI) policies in two music history classes at a mid-sized public university in the United States. During the course of creating the policies, students educated one another about the benefits and drawbacks of GenAI, reflected on their own GenAI use, and articulated their collective position on GenAI in the music history classroom. Outcomes suggest that student-instructor partnerships can serve as a powerful tool in ensuring the ethical and thoughtful use of GenAI.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Decolonizing students as partners
abstract: Realizing the transformative potential of students-as-partners (SaP) requires expanding existing partnership frameworks through a diverse, explicitly decolonial knowledge base. Working from a student-faculty research partnership context, this review engages Cook-Sather et al.’s (2014) 3Rs and Matthews’ (2017) five propositions for SaP by weaving in principles from the 5Rs of Indigenous education (Restoule, 2018; Tessaro et al., 2018) and the 6Rs of Indigenous research (Tsosie et al., 2022). Drawing on multidisciplinary and Indigenous literatures, we reconceptualize six core principles for transformational partnerships (Respect, Reciprocity, Responsibility, Relevance, Relationships, and Representation) and formalize a seventh principle (Reflection). This enriched set of seven SaP principles (7Rs) offers a wholistic framework to inform genuine collaborations across research, teaching, and learning contexts. This conceptual review productively disrupts Western colonial assumptions in the scholarship of teaching and learning (SoTL), demonstrating that integrating Indigenous worldviews advances decolonial SaP theory and practice, supporting more relational, transformative student-facult

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Belonging and collaboration in clinical education
abstract: Effective clinical education depends on strong student–educator partnerships, yet the processes that support or hinder these relationships remain poorly understood. This study examined perspectives of clinical educators (CEs) and students on fostering belonging in clinical education. Members of the Student-Instructor Partnerships in Clinical Education (SIPCE) learning community, representing diverse health professions, participated in focus groups. Discussions explored definitions of belonging, barriers to partnership, and strategies for strengthening relationships. Thematic analysis revealed key facilitators, including recognition of both students and CEs as whole people, active engagement, and timely, constructive feedback. Barriers included power imbalances, role ambiguity, and students’ fear of failure. Mutual respect, empathy, and intentional collaboration were identified as essential for effective partnerships. Positive relationships enhanced confidence, engagement, and willingness to take learning risks, while barriers constrained outcomes. Findings highlight the importance of addressing power dynamics and fostering trust to optimize clinical learning environments.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Building a STEM peer mentor program with students as partners
abstract: We analyze a science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) peer mentor program using the students-as-partners (SaP) propositions proposed by Matthews (2017). The data consists of student worker testimonials and documented experiences, staff experiences with the program, and surveys. While the partnership with student workers in the program aligns with most of the five tenets, “uncertain outcomes” and “partnership for transformation” are only partially implemented as defined by Matthews. The program successfully meets its stated outcome, and the partnership with student workers is instrumental in achieving it. Additionally, the student workers benefit from working in a less hierarchical relationship. We propose that SaP is a helpful approach to analyze the role of student workers as it allows for understanding how students may develop in said less hierarchical working relationship and for evaluating the strengths and shortcomings of specific implementations. Future studies applying a similar approach could move the field towards a more unified theoretical framework. It will be important to establish which tenets are central, what benefits students receive under which cond

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Disabled students as partners
abstract: This case study introduces a staff-student partnership project about reasonable adjustment (accommodations) policy and practice in one university in England. The project involved interviews and focus groups with 83 members of the university community and influenced the implementation plan for the institution’s revised adjustment policy, including the establishment of a Disabled Student Champion role in each department and a university-wide network to support it. The paper, written together by staff and student leads, outlines the project findings and impact while addressing the partners’ project reflections. These highlight the tension between partnership and representation, suggest that project management norms need to be critically questioned, and point to the importance of trust, reflexivity, care, and valuing different ways of contributing to inclusive partnership work. Against a backdrop of the marginalization of disabled students in higher education decision-making, the case study provides an example of how a partnership approach can influence institutional change.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: A scenario analysis on the transformative potential of student partnerships and co-creation in fostering belonging in student support
abstract: This case study examines how student-staff partnerships and co-creation can transform student belonging by evaluating and improving support in higher education. The case study reflects upon the development of the ABC Toolkit, created collaboratively and guides improvements to support practices throughout the student journey. Three pillars—Academic Anchoring, Belonging and Well-being, and Co-creation and Communication—provide practical methods for creating inclusive, timely, and student-centered interventions that strengthen belonging and institutional responsiveness. Recognizing students as experts in their own experiences, the project incorporated a student partner as an equal member of the research team. Based on partnership models, the study shows how collaborative evaluation fosters inclusive, responsive support and empowers both staff and students Co-creation enhances team dynamics, research outcomes, and shared ownership . Based at a United Kingdom university, the findings offer insights relevant internationally, especially for diversity and inclusion challenges. The study contributes to Students-as-Partners literature by demonstrating how authentic partnerships can improve i

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Relational agency in student partnerships
abstract: This paper seeks to connect the theory of relational agency with students as partners (SaP) research and practice. Relational agency is a theory that defines agency as emerging through working with others within a particular activity system. In SaP work, students enacting agency is seen as a marker of success for the partnership; however, the focus is often on an individual’s experiences of agency. Through modeling the co-construction of ideas and objects, relational agency places agency as a feature of interaction rather than an attribute of the individual. By bringing relational agency into conversation with SaP, we introduce a lens for recognizing agency within partnerships between students and staff/faculty, as well as the capacity that is built through such partnerships.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: "It makes us feel important"
abstract: This case study explores interview data from four students involved in students-as-partners (SaP) projects during an International Foundation Program (IFP) at a university in the UK. The projects included developing a week of study-support sessions, writing for the Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) committee, and writing for the university’s blog. The students worked with staff members in different ways and were interviewed about their motivations, challenges, benefits, and recommendations for future student-staff projects. The interview data suggest that the projects aligned well with the partnership values of reciprocity and trust (Higher Education Academy, 2015). As a result, the projects seemed to contribute to students’ sense of belonging to the IFP learning community as well as the wider institution. Future iterations of SaP projects on the IFP should endeavor to more closely align with the value of inclusivity (Higher Education Academy, 2015) by adopting more accessible recruitment processes.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Institutional perspectives on Students as Partners
abstract: The importance of institutional context on the shape and practice of Students as Partners (SaP) is well acknowledged. However, to date, there has been limited investigation into how institutional factors influence SaP programs and practice. This paper addresses this gap through a comparative case study analysis of Students as Partners at two research-intensive universities. Drawing on institutional documents, web materials, and teaching and learning publications, our analysis applies Bolman and Deal’s (2021) Four Frames analysis to our two contexts. Further, through institutional metaphors, we highlight how SaP has taken root as a centralized organism at one campus, compared to a distributed ecology at the other, an analysis that can help practitioners understand the most fertile institutional ground for their own SaP initiatives. This study contributes to SaP scholarship by offering a novel theoretical lens for leaders and practitioners to conceptualize institutional influence on student partnership programs.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: The frameworks partners bring to students-as-partners work

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Portraying partnership
abstract: In this reflective essay, the author describes their experience utilizing multimodal facilitation strategies during weekly meetings of student consultants working with faculty partners in Students as Teachers and Learners, a pedagogical partnership program at Bryn Mawr and Haverford Colleges. By responding to three imaginative exercises that leveraged the affordances of multiple modalities, student partners were able to reflect upon the multifacetedness of their pedagogical partnership experience, deepening their understanding of the complexity and diversity of partnership work.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: From interpreters to partners
abstract: Identity-based tasks can transform students from passive recipients to active partners in cross-cultural language settings. This case study demonstrates such a transformation by introducing the pedagogical framework, Guo’s Triangular Activation Model (GTAM), which effectively integrates purpose-driven, identity-based, and context-embedded learning. Originally developed in China and later adapted in Canadian settings, the framework has been applied across K–12 (kindergarten through Grade 12) and postsecondary contexts. As a result, across these contexts, students moved from passive recipients to active contributors, demonstrating cultural agency, ownership, and motivation. This progression showsthat activating student identity fosters relational engagement and complex learning, aligning with the students-as-partners (SaP) approach. The paper reflects on how identity-based tasks can build authentic partnerships between educators and students. The study offers implications for adapting this identity-based framework to diverse cultural and institutional settings. It also discusses how meaningful, task-driven roles can deepen student participation.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Student-led reflection cycles to support faculty instructional improvement
abstract: We report on a student-faculty partnership in which trained student-researchers guide faculty toward instructional improvement through a professional development format known as reflection cycles. Reflection cycles are guided by a student-developed, literature-informed tool to support faculty in goal setting and reflecting on equity-minded active learning in mathematics. Faculty participants reported benefiting from guided reflection, specialized student knowledge, accountability, support with new strategies, and non-evaluative observation. They also noted room for improvement through additional challenge, more feedback, more follow-up, and additional support with strategies. Our research reveals that faculty are willing to learn from students and that students have valuable perspectives to offer to faculty. We suggest that reflection cycles can allow all instructors, regardless of prior knowledge, confidence, or experience, to work gradually and continuously to improve their instruction at a sustainable pace. Through student-guided reflection, faculty can work towards a more equity-minded active classroom and address longstanding opportunity gaps in mathematics.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Undergraduate nursing students’ and faculty’s perceptions of remediation resource co-design
abstract: The development of student-focused remediation resources aligns well with students-as-partners approaches, particularly co-design. However, there is limited research exploring co-design in nursing education, and few studies, if any, have examined its use in the development of remediation resources to support clinical placements. This study aimed to explore nursing students' and faculty's perceptions of co-designed remediation resources to support clinical placements. Co-design involved framing the problem through a literature review, student surveys and a focus group; planning and designing the co-designed remediation resources and strategies; and trialling the co-designed remediation outputs. A qualitative, exploratory design was used, involving thematic analysis of students' and faculty's written reflections on the co-design of remediation resources. Participants perceived co-design positively. Four overarching themes were identified, including confidence as co-design evolves; enhanced collaboration and awareness; feeling cared for and connected; and ongoing benefits for oneself and others. Co-design with nursing students and faculty is a feasible, student-focused approach to dev

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Students as partners for learning analytics
abstract: While learning analytics has shown promise to enhance student learning, culturally specific ethical considerations on how students would like their data to be used need to be investigated and included in institutional implementation. This joint study with student researchers from both a United Kingdom-based and an Asian university employed mixed approaches to understand how students 1) use data for learning, 2) view data privacy, and 3) perceive the usefulness of learning analytics for enhancing their student experience. We found that most students in both contexts are concerned about privacy and would like clarity and autonomy over what, how, and with whom their data are shared. In addition, the paper presents the reflections on working with students as partners, identifies this approach as an essential and effective way to enculturate students in data ethics and to gather authentic, context-specific student voices to shape policies around learning analytics.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: The Initiative for Students as Partners in Research and Education (InSPiRE)
abstract: The Initiative for Students as Partners in Research and Education (InSPiRE) research team and its work on the Second-Year Experience (SYE) project at The University of Texas at Austin (UT) created new opportunities for the Center for Teaching and Learning (CTL) to engage in student-centered co-curricular learning and research. Prior to their involvement in the InSPiRE team, none of the undergraduate students had experience with moving from initial conceptualizations of a social science research question through the stage of making their research public. By centering community, valuing process as product, embracing methodological pluralism, and making research labor visible, InSPiRE engaged CTL staff and university leaders and shaped conversations about the SYE and student success. In this case study, we use personal narratives to excavate central characteristics of the InSPiRE research and community-building process.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Students as partners
abstract: This study contributes to the growing literature on students as partners (SaP) by centering undergraduate voices in the evaluation of virtual reality (VR) simulation-based learning in a speech-language pathology (SLP) practicum course. Three student-researchers engaged in narrative reflection to explore how their clinical personas developed, what changed due to the simulation experience, and the perceived advantages and limitations. Reflections were thematically analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s (2022) framework, emphasizing student agency and shared meaning-making. Unlike prior research focused solely on skill acquisition, this study highlighted the value of collaborative inquiry in shaping clinical identity and adaptive reasoning. The integration of immersive VR simulations, commonly used in teacher education, into clinical SLP training demonstrated the broader applicability of simulation-based learning. The findings underscore the potential of SaP frameworks to foster inclusive, equity-driven pedagogies and inform global best practices. Ultimately, this research has affirmed the transformative impact of student-faculty partnerships on learning, teaching, and the development of i

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: The power of pivoting
abstract: This case study examines the production of "The call," an episode of We Met U When…, a podcastproduced by journalism students at Toronto Metropolitan University. It illustrates how a curriculum co-creation approach that treats students as colleagues and a willingness to seize opportunities created by unforeseen events facilitated a pivot away from a planned assignment and led to deeper learning. During an interview, a student experienced a microaggression that was captured in the recording. The class collaboratively decided to pivot from the original subject and produce an episode about the impact of microaggressions. The instructor’s approach builds on the concept of radical collegiality, which challenges the idea that students are not colleagues (Lubicz-Nawrocka, 2018). This case study, co-authored by the instructor and a student-producer, demonstrates the power of going off plan, taking risks in teaching, and giving students agency.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Preliminary identification of barriers and facilitators to students as partners work
abstract: A learning community (LC) was convened that included university educators and learners to explore perspectives on students-as-partners (SaP) work on the university’s campus. The LC was facilitated by one educator and two learners. The qualitative data identified potential barriers to SaP, including learners’ views that the success or failure of this work was entirely dependent on educators, while the educators were concerned about managing power dynamics and challenges in engaging students in partnerships. Facilitators of SaP work on campus were identified as creating open lines of communication, fostering effective working relationships, and developing a sense of mutuality in which all participants were seen as having equal value in the partnership.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Co-creating reflective pedagogy
abstract: This case study explores the transformative role of a student-staff partnership (SSP) in redesigning assessment and learning experiences for the core master’s-level course, Global Challenges in Agriculture (AGRC7047). At the heart of this initiative was a diverse team of student and staff partners who co-developed new learning materials and assessment structures to better engage a heterogeneous cohort. A key outcome of this collaboration was the design and implementation of a reflexive ePortfolio assessment. This innovation emerged from the SSP’s commitment to inclusivity, pedagogical alignment, and global citizenship education. Rather than positioning the ePortfolio as the central course, this paper foregrounds the SSP process: how students and staff worked as co-creators, how diverse disciplinary and cultural perspectives enriched the project, and how this model can inform broader efforts to co-create curriculum in agricultural sciences and beyond. By documenting the application of SSP within agricultural sciences, an area where partnership-based pedagogical research remains limited, this study contributes new insights into how co-creation can reshape teaching practices in applie

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Creating the conditions for partnership
abstract: This case study describes how a Dutch teacher education program brought students as partners (SaP) principles to life during a major curriculum renewal. Five development teams, comprising staff, field professionals, and student developers, collaborated across 10 co-design days. Students were prepared through workshops on dialogue and decision-making, followed by collective reflection after each session. Using SaP dimensions such as engagement, equity, reflexivity, and ownership clarified what partnership looked like in practice. The process fostered trust, mutual learning, and belonging among all participants. Staff perspectives on curriculum design shifted, and students gained confidence to contribute meaningfully. Early indicators showed reduced student attrition, and the collaboration led to a SaP coordination team to sustain the work. We reflect on key enabling conditions such as time, structure, and relational trust, and discuss dilemmas related to power and workload. Our experience offers encouragement and practical insights for embedding SaP more deeply in curriculum design.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Assessing the impact of a student-faculty pedagogical partnership to infuse equity and improve the student learning experience at a minority-serving institution
abstract: This study examined the impact of a student–faculty pedagogical partnership by collecting evidence on whether enrolled students at a minority-serving institution perceived and experienced faculty-implemented changes made in response to their learning needs. Undergraduate student partners gathered feedback in three introductory humanities courses and discussed student perspectives with respective course faculty to inform instruction. Near the end of the term, SATAL student partners administered a six-question impact survey, first individually and then in groups of three to five students, to collect the class’s reactions to the faculty’s interventions. Qualitative and quantitative findings indicated that most enrolled students (>80%) observed the implemented changes and expressed satisfaction with the faculty's response to their feedback. Students’ open-ended responses were analyzed following Saldaña’s (2015) coding process. Students described how the changes “encouraged a more open and respectful exchange of ideas” and helped create an environment where “everyone felt comfortable participating and building new connections.” This assessment article, co-authored by staff, students, an

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: From fragmentation to resilience
abstract: This case study examines a mentored autoethnography co-developed by a neuroscience and physiology major and a counselor-educator at a Jesuit university in the United States. Integrating science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and creative reflection, the student produced fourteen paired artworks and journals during weekly mentoring sessions guided by the Ignatian pedagogical paradigm and its emphasis on cura personalis, or holistic care. Check-ins, collaborative analysis, and shared authorship supported a learning environment that balanced intellectual challenge with emotional safety. The findings illustrate the student’s movement from fragmentation toward resilience and agency. The case contributes to students-as-partners (SaP) literature by demonstrating how arts-based inquiry can function as a participatory and relational mode of co-inquiry. Through shared meaning-making and co-analysis, the partners enacted core SaP principles, including reciprocity, reflexivity, and shared authority. The mentoring framework expands current SaP models by integrating expressive arts as a medium for partnership-based knowledge building and supporting authentic relational engageme

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Perception of students as partners in learning among students and faculty members of the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery, Karachi, Pakistan
abstract: This study explores perceptions of the students-as-partners approach in nursing education among students and faculty at the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery, Karachi, Pakistan. The approach has gained prominence in higher education for fostering active engagement, mutual respect, and collaborative knowledge construction, making it highly relevant in nursing, where theory and practice must align. This study contributes to the limited body of literature on students as partners (SaP) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) by offering an original perspective that incorporates student, faculty, and leadership voices within a hierarchical, resource-constrained context. This study used, with 120 participants (80 students and 40 faculty) completing a structured questionnaire and open-ended questions. We adopted a qualitative descriptive exploratory design to remain close to participants’ accounts while systematically describing patterns salient to the local context. The findings revealed that 85% of students and 90% of faculty expressed a favorable view of the approach, highlighting benefits such as improved critical thinking, enhanced communication, and stronger mu

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Reflective insights on co-creating an elective course as students as partners

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Enhancing digital teaching and learning
abstract: The following article presents a review and reflection on digital teaching, learning, and assessment (TL&A) in higher education (HE) in the context of the emergency pivot to online delivery during the pandemic, as experienced by the Enhancing Digital Teaching and Learning (EDTL) student interns across multiple disciplines and institutions. The project was led by the Irish Universities Association (IUA, https://www.iua.ie/ourwork/learning-teaching/digital-learning/) and funded by the Irish Higher Education Authority (HEA, https://hea.ie/). Additionally, this review draws upon previous literature related to successful staff-student partnerships, advocating the inclusion of the student voice in all aspects of teaching and learning, specifically in relation to the adoption of digital technologies, assessment, and teaching strategies within education. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the original interns (n=7) representing HE universities in Ireland in 2021. Key findings from this study highlight a strong sense of inclusion, partnership and collaboration within each intern’s institution.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Creation and nurturing of staff-student partnerships
abstract: While the pedagogical benefits of Staff-Student Partnerships (SSP) and Students as Partners (SaP) are widely recognized, the complex and often invisible challenges of initiating and sustaining such collaborations remain underexplored. This reflective essay critically examines the unspoken dimensions that shape SSP/SaP practices across diverse institutional and cultural contexts. Drawing on our lived experiences and collaborative inquiry, we explore four provocations: the challenge of achieving conceptual clarity across institutions; the generative potential of uncertainty in partnership work; the often-overlooked emotional labor involved; and the systemic resistance to transformative change. Rather than offering solutions, we invite the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) community into deeper dialogue about the paradoxes, tensions, and lived realities of co-creation in higher education. By highlighting these underexplored aspects, we aim to foster more honest, inclusive, and critically engaged conversations about partnership practices in teaching and learning.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: Transformation from learning to co-creating knowledge with teachers
abstract: Higher education is shifting from traditional teaching models to participatory approaches that emphasize student engagement and collaboration. The students as partners (SaP) framework redefines the student-teacher relationship, positioning students as co-creators of knowledge. This study explores a student’s transition from conventional learning to co-creation in the department of education at Aga Khan University in Pakistan. The paper examines perspectives of both students and teachers. Using an exploratory case study, this study focuses on a student who engaged in SaP at both the undergraduate and graduate levels and later collaborated professionally with the same teachers. Data from student reflections and interviews with three educators highlight SaP’s transformative potential to foster engagement, innovation, and mutual learning. The study contributes empirical insights into how partnership can evolve relationally and professionally beyond formal coursework as well as highlights the considerations necessary for more equitable and contextually responsive implementation.

journal_name: International Journal for Students as Partners
title: The added value of equitable multistakeholder co-creation in higher education
abstract: Co-creation in higher education (HE) involving students, teachers, and working field professionals can lead to innovative solutions for complex issues. In seven cases, equitable multistakeholder co-creation has been examined. Participants (N=52) completed a survey with open-ended questions and participated in interviews. We found that equitable co-creation led to a strong feeling of involvement, a better understanding of other perspectives, ideas for solutions, and the professionalization of all stakeholders. Students felt heard, experienced growing self-confidence, gained deeper insights into their future professional field, and expanded their professional network. Teachers gained inspiration to enrich and rewrite their curricula content and lesson activities. Working field professionals found innovative ideas for their practice, discovered new possibilities to find partners with whom sustainable development plans could be set out, and experienced feelings of satisfaction by contributing to the development of students. Supporting and hindering factors for equitable co-creation and implications for HE are discussed.
